Figure 1. Comparison of video understanding paradigms: (a) Single Forward of model with one-off context selection. (b) Retrieval-Based
Video Agent. (c) LensWalk, an agent framework that actively plans observations to fulfill subsequent reasoning, explores iteratively, and
self-regulates its observation budget. (d) By actively planning observations only on video segments essential to its reasoning process,
LensWalk simultaneously achieves high accuracy and exceptional efficiency.

   To this end, we present LensWalk, an agentic frame-
work that gives the LLM reasoner on-hand control over                            Our empirical results on long video understanding and
where, and how dense to look at the video for active ob-                     video reasoning benchmarks reveal that this framework is
servation. LensWalk organizes inference as a multi-round                     not only conceptually appealing but also practically effec-
reason–plan–observe loop: at each round, the reasoner re-                    tive. As a plug-and-play agentic framework, LensWalk con-
flects on the current question and accumulated evidence,                     sistently improves even strong Reasoner–Observer combi-
then plans an observation action by selecting an observa-                    nations; when a single model serves as both to make self-
tion tool and its parameters, which determine the visible                    scheduled observation, it effectively offers a “free lunch”,
context—which temporal regions of the source video to in-                    yielding substantial gains—for example, the powerful o3
spect and at what sampling level. This loop is instantiated                  model improves by over 11.5% and 6.7% accuracy on
by a suite of complementary observation tools powered by                     challenging long-video benchmarks such as LVBench and
a vision-language model that converts the prepared context                   VideoMME (long split). At the same time, LensWalk ex-
into visual evidence: Scan Search supports parallel sweeps                   hibits an emergent ability to manage observational cost: it
over broad, disjoint candidate ranges for cue discovery, Seg-                adaptively resolves easy queries with minimal turns, while
ment Focus constructs compact, detail-oriented views for a                   allocating more budget only to genuinely uncertain cases,
targeted interval, and Stitched Verify assembles custom sam-                 as in Figure 1(d), leading to total token usage far below
ples from multiple key segments into a single context for                    that of retrieval agents that consume millions of tokens and
global checking. Each tool is encouraged to return frame-                    only slightly above a single dense pass over long frame se-
interleaved timestamps aligned with discovered key infor-                    quences. Analysis of its reasoning traces further reveals di-
mation as anchors for subsequent rounds. As observations                     verse, human-like strategies—strategic reflection, progres-
are acquired progressively from raw video, LensWalk main-                    sive zoom-in, and integrative verification—replacing the

Figure 2. Illustration of LensWalk’s reasoning-scheduled active observation on a real trace. The LLM reasoner alternates Scan Search and
Segment Focus to seek question-relevant evidence, initially misclassifies a mole as the queried water vole and records conflicting memories
in the subject table (red text), then invokes Stitch Verify to inspect key segments, resolve the contradiction, and arrive at the correct answer.

Figure 4. Tool-call behavior of LensWalk across model recipes, visualized following [63]. We group behaviour into six strategy types
and show their ratio (sector angle), average frame cost (dashed polygon), and accuracy (noted as score; sector radius), revealing adaptive
allocation of more frames to harder queries and diverse exploration under uncertainty.

step. We categorize these patterns into six primary modes                                                                                                 gic Reflection or Integrative Verify to expand and consol-
(in Figure 4, see Appendix C for details and examples.):                                                                                                  idate evidence. These recovery mechanisms yield more
Direct Inquiry. Resolving a task in a single, confident step                                                                                              stable and higher accuracy than the rare looping failures
without prior exploration, typically for high-level or tempo-                                                                                             that remain.
rally anchored questions.                                                                                                                               • Observer quality shapes strategy and efficiency. For
    Progressive Zoom-in. Starting from a broad scan to lo-                                                                                                a fixed Reasoner, the Observer’s capability is a critical
cate candidate moments and then zooming into promising                                                                                                    performance driver. A strong Observer (e.g., o3) sup-
segments for more detailed inspection.                                                                                                                    plies clear, decisive evidence that directly addresses the
    Scope Partitioning. Partitioning the timeline into dis-                                                                                               query’s intent, enabling frequent, low-cost Direct Inquiry.
tinct scopes, analyzing them independently, and integrating                                                                                               In contrast, weaker Observers (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-72B)
the resulting insights purely at the reasoning level to form a                                                                                            introduce ambiguity, pushing the agent into more com-
conclusion.                                                                                                                                               plex and expensive observation plans such as retreating
    Strategic Reflection. After a focused search hits a dead                                                                                              to broader scans or repeated verification. This gap high-

broader scan over alternative regions or hypotheses.                                                                                                      effective reasoning.

jointly inspecting multiple key moments in a single stitched                                                                                            5. Conclusion
observation, enabling holistic confirmation of the conclu-
sion.                                                                                                                                                   In this work, we introduced LensWalk, an agentic frame-
    Static Repetition. Falling into an unproductive cycle of                                                                                            work that actively scheduled video observation based on
nearly identical observations over the same region with a                                                                                               reasoning in each iteration. By granting a language model
static intent, showing little progress or change in strategy.                                                                                           the ability to dynamically control what to see, and at
    Analysis of these patterns reveals several key findings:                                                                                            what granularity, LensWalk transforms video understand-
• Difficulty-aware cost allocation. The agent intuitively                                                                                               ing from a static recognition task into an adaptive reason-
   allocates more observational effort to challenging prob-                                                                                             plan-observe loop. This design not only yields substan-
   lems. Hard questions with lower accuracy are associated                                                                                              tial, plug-and-play performance gains across diverse multi-
   with longer, more costly observation traces, while sim-                                                                                              modal models and long-video benchmarks, but also uncov-
   ple cases are often resolved efficiently with less frames or                                                                                         ers emergent cognitive behaviors such as progressive zoom-
   even single-step inquiries. This indicates that LensWalk                                                                                             in, reflective replanning, and integrative verification. Our
   adapts its observation depth based on the evolving uncer-                                                                                            findings highlight that scalable video intelligence lies not
   tainty of each query.                                                                                                                                only in ever-larger frozen representations, but in scalable vi-
• Emergent reflective strategies replace inefficient loops.                                                                                             sual cognition—where observation is actively orchestrated
   Empowered by diverse choices in its observation plan, the                                                                                            by reasoning intent. We believe LensWalk provides a con-
   agent largely avoids the “Static Repetition” behaviour re-                                                                                           crete step towards the next generation of self-directed mul-
   ported in prior work[43, 62]. When faced with uncer-                                                                                                 timodal agents, capable of learning how to observe as they
   tainty, it instead invokes reflective patterns such as Strate-                                                                                       think, and ultimately, how to think through seeing.

 Algorithm 1: LensWalk Reason–Plan-Observe loop with Subject Table Memory update.
  Input : Video V , query Q, metadata Vinfo , tool set O = {Scan Search, Segment Focus, Stitched Verify, Finish}, max
             steps Tmax
  Output: Answer to Q
  Initialize history L0 ← {Q, Vinfo };
  Initialize subject table Sub0 ← ∅;
  for t = 1, 2, . . . , Tmax do
       at = (ot , qt , It , ρot ) ← Mr (Q, Vinfo , Lt−1 , Subt−1 );
       if ot = Finish then
            return qt as final answer;
       Gt ← BuildContextGroups(ot , It , ρot );            // Maps tool-level sampling arguments into
        VLM-visible context groups
                        (k)     (k)              (k)                                               (k)
       // Gt = {(It , st )}K
                           k=1 , where It
                             t
                                          is the k-th time interval and st collects
          its sampling settings (e.g., fps, frame budget)
       // Kt = 1 for Segment Focus and Stitched Verify; Kt > 1 (parallel slices) for
          Scan Search
                  (k)     (k)
       for each (It , st ) ∈ Gt do
             (k)                   (k) (k)                                             (k)

                                    (k)
           sampling config st
           (k)            (k) (k)

                         (k)

                              t
                                         // Simple join: concatenate per-group replies in
         temporal order into a single observation string
       Lt ← Lt−1 ∪ {(at , et )};
       if subject memory enabled then
            Subt ← MemoryUpdate(Subt−1 , at , et );
       else
           Subt ← Subt−1 ;
   return unknown;

You are a helpful assistant designed to answer multi-step questions about video content by sequentially invoking tools for
video observation. Your sole purpose is to reason and act to uncover the correct answer. Operate in a rigorous THINK → PLAN

→ OBSERVE loop with at most MAX_CALL tool calls.

THINK: Based on the user’s query and all previous observations, reason step by step about what is known, what is uncertain, and
what to do next. Justify the next action by stating the goal, the best tool, chosen time ranges, and the sampling strategy (e.g., higher

FPS for fast actions, lower for context).

ACT: Call exactly one video observation tool with the decided parameters. Time ranges and sampling intensity should match the
planned evidence needs, avoiding both information loss and redundancy.

OBSERVE: Use the returned structured observation to update understanding and continue the next THINK cycle.

Continue until you have sufficient evidence, then call finish with the final answer.

Core directives: (1) Never guess; inspect the video when uncertain. (2) Plan within frame budget. (3) Iterate and refine. (4) Verify
and synthesize after multiple related segments. (5) Ground arguments in evidence; do not invent timestamps.


                                     Figure 5. System prompt used for the LensWalk Reasoner.


Based on your observations and tool outputs, provide a concise answer that directly addresses the question. Only provide the
option’s letter from the given choices as the final answer for multiple-choice questions.
Total video length: VIDEO_LENGTH seconds.
Question: QUESTION_PLACEHOLDER


                                        Figure 6. User prompt used for LensWalk Reasoner.


You are a highly focused visual understanding assistant. Your task is to analyze a short sequence of sparsely sampled video frames
from a single segment and assess its relevance to the user’s query. You need to provide a concise summary of the visual content
and explain why it is, or is not, related to the query.
IMPORTANT: Your scope is strictly limited to the provided frames from this single segment. Your conclusion must be based only
on what is visible here. Do not make any assumptions about the rest of the video or events outside these frames. Your response
should be a brief, self-contained analysis of this segment’s relevance.


                                       Figure 7. Prompt for the Observer in Scan Search tool.


You are a meticulous and factual video analysis assistant. Your task is to analyze a set of sparsely sampled frames from a single,
continuous time segment of a video. Provide a detailed and objective description that directly answers the user’s query.
IMPORTANT: Base your entire analysis strictly on the visual information present in the frames provided. The frames are sampled
uniformly. Do not infer or imagine events happening beyond the frames. Your output should be a concise and structured text
focused solely on the evidence at hand.


                                     Figure 8. Prompt for the Observer in Segment Focus tool.
   You are an expert video analyst specializing in synthesizing information from multiple, distinct key moments. You will be shown a
   “stitched” collection of frames sampled from various, potentially non-contiguous time intervals of a video. Your goal is to provide
   a cohesive analysis that addresses the user’s query, drawing connections or noting changes between the different moments shown.
   IMPORTANT: The frames represent a curated, sparse, and non-uniform selection. Do not assume what happens in the time gaps
   between the provided segments. Base your entire analysis strictly on the visual evidence presented, treating each time-stamped
   group as a distinct snapshot.


                              Figure 9. Prompt for the Observer in Stitched Verify tool (stitched_observer).


   Memory role. You are a specialized assistant responsible for maintaining a subject_registry for a video analysis agent.
   You analyze the latest observation and its subjects, compare them against the existing registry, and produce a consolidated registry
   only (no narrative summary).
   Input provided.
   • Current subject registry (master list so far).
   • History: past tool calls and their results.
   • Current turn: latest tool call, its raw output, and a [new observed subject registry] extracted from that call.
   Update rules.
   1. Merge by synthesis, not stacking. When updating a subject’s description list, synthesize concise, high-value descriptions
      instead of appending redundant strings. Example: from “man in red shirt” and “man in red shirt, sitting at desk” produce “man

      in red shirt” and “sitting at desk” (or “man in red shirt (was standing, now sitting at desk)”), not duplicated phrases.
   2. Add new subjects when they cannot be merged.
   3. Prune to the 15 most recently observed. After merge/add, keep at most 15 subjects prioritized by most recent appearance,
      giving current-turn subjects highest priority.
   4. No subjects ⇒ output an empty object {}.
   Output format (single JSON object).
   {
       " updated_subject_registry ": {
          "A u n i q u e and c o n s i s t e n t i d e n t i f i e r f o r a s u b j e c t " : {
            " description ": [


                 " Key a p p e a r a n c e / r o l e / s t a t e s t r i n g s ( e . g . ,   ' man i n r e d s h i r t ' ,   ' s i t t i n g at
           desk ' , ' t a l k i n g t o S2 ' ) . "
              ],
              " appeared_intervals ": [
                 "[ s t a r t _ s e c , end_sec ]"
              ]
           }
       }
   }

C.2. Behaviour Analysis
Section 4.4 has introduced the taxonomy of tool-call be-
                                                                    Strategic Reflection. Strategic Reflection is a higher-
havior patterns; this section provides a detailed analysis of
                                                                    level reasoning pattern in which the agent realizes that its
representative instances for each behavior.
                                                                    current observational strategy is failing, then backtracks
                                                                    to explore broader temporal regions before refining again,
Direct Inquiry. Direct Inquiry is the simplest tool-use             rather than over-focusing on an uninformative segment. As
pattern, where the agent can answer with only one or two            illustrated in Fig. 15, once the model recognizes that the
tool calls. It is mainly used for straightforward temporal-         subtitles in the initial interval do not explain the game rules,
localization questions such as “What happens at the begin-          it strategically shifts to another part of the video, enabling it
ning of the video?” or “What occurs between 10:21 and               to observe the optimal game strategy and ultimately obtain
10:25?”, as well as questions about the overall video type.         the correct answer.

Scope Partitioning. Scope Partitioning adopts a divide-               the video.
and-conquer strategy: the agent partitions the video into
coarse segments and sequentially checks whether each re-              C.3. Failure Modes and Analysis
gion contains clues worth closer inspection. As shown in
                                                                      In this section, we illustrate a few failure modes observed
Fig. 16, it first scans the intervals 0–600s, 600–1200s, and
                                                                      during our evaluation. Analyzing these error patterns pro-
1200–1800s to locate the position of the clue about the third
                                                                      vides valuable insights into the limitations of current Large
set, then identifies 1200–1800s as the most promising range,
                                                                      Language Models (LLMs) acting as reasoning planners and
performs more fine-grained observations there, and finally
                                                                      highlights critical directions for future active video agent
derives the correct answer.
                                                                      design. We identify four primary failure patterns:
                                                                      Premature Conclusion. The agent terminates the reason-
Static Repetition. In contrast to Strategic Reflection,               ing loop too early (often within 1–2 turns) upon encounter-
Static Repetition denotes a rigid mode in which the model             ing the most frequent cue “pyramid complex” in the initial
becomes trapped in an unproductive strategy. Rather than              observation, as shown in Fig. 18. By failing to validate this
exploring alternative temporal regions or adjusting its ob-           cue against potential distractors or cross-reference it with
servation queries, it repeatedly issues nearly identical ob-          other video segments, the model exhibits unwarranted over-
serve calls with the same intent on the same segment, even            confidence. This failure mode suggests that future agents
after multiple failed attempts to find supporting evidence, as        require a stronger internal “critic” or verification mecha-
shown in Fig. 17. This fixation on a single interval prevents         nism to balance token efficiency with rigorous hypothesis
the model from discovering the correct answer elsewhere in            testing.
Evidence Dilution. Conversely, excessive observation can
degrade performance. We observe cases, as in Fig. 19,
where the agent discovers strong, decisive evidence in early
turns e.g. “STRENGTH UNDER PRESSURE” or “MEN-
TAL ABILITY”, to the correct choice “Mental ability and
vast experience”, but continues to explore irrelevant seg-
ments. As the context window fills with “loose” or noisy
information, the strong initial evidence gets diluted. The
agent finally succumbs to recency bias or confusion, hal-
lucinating an answer based on the latest weak observations.
This underscores the importance of active memory manage-
ment—agents must learn not just when to seek information,
but when to prune irrelevant context to maintain reasoning
clarity.
Persistent Ambiguity. The agent may persistently search
along an uninformative trajectory and never obtain decisive
visual evidence, ultimately being forced to give an ambigu-
ous, semantics-only guess rather than a visually grounded
answer. As shown in Fig. 20, the agent keeps focusing
on related subtitles instead of frame-wise visual changes,
misses the key opening event, and therefore predicts incor-
rectly.
Static Repetition. Finally, as noted in the behavioral anal-
ysis, the agent may fall into a degenerate loop, repeatedly
issuing identical tool calls for the same timestamp without
adjusting its parameters. This reflects a failure in the agent’s
meta-cognition or state tracking; the planner fails to recog-
nize that its current strategy is unproductive, highlighting
the need for mechanisms that detect stagnation and trigger
strategic shifts (e.g., from Segment Focus to Strategic Re-
flection).
